pillar_reactions.evidence: Delivered first and tied to his own sports — 'you're not just building strength, you're building conditioning and mobility at the same time, and it doesn't require hours of training. It's 30, 40 minutes, three, four times a week', then 'in your specific case, that will definitely help you also in endurance racing, but... you mentioned surfing, right?' Andy did not merely accept it, he ran with it and supplied his own supporting case: 'that's the other thing I liked about kettlebells is that they combine both the metabolic... I've worn my watch and I'm up to 150, 160... it's interval training, right?' and then connected it to surfing himself — 'that's the other time I felt that, trying to paddle out to the outside in big waves. It's constant, it's just brutal.' Caveat for the coach: the rep's mobility promise was generic ('wherever you have weak points, he will focus on that') and never touched the two hip replacements, which is the one place a specific answer would have landed.

The rep pre-conceded the pillar before delivering it — 'second thing is nutrition, but, in your case, actually, nutrition is already good, yeah, it's dialed in, pretty solid' — then gave the three-variable version anyway (what you eat, when you eat, how much; clean food, a 10-to-8-hour eating window, quantity taking care of itself). Andy raised no questions and no objection, which is unsurprising given he already tracks macros at about 130g protein a day and has a sports-science student for a son. Accepted rather than enthusiastic: no positive reaction was volunteered and no tie to his own goal was made. Note the missed opening — Andy said he had just swapped from high-fat/low-carb to higher carb on his 17-year-old son's advice and was unsure, which was a live nutrition question the pillar could have answered and did not.

Fully delivered: direct access to Trevor including his phone number, an instruction to over-communicate, a bespoke written plan off a one-to-one call, weekly check-ins covering sleep and stress, video form review until movements are locked in, and everything organised in TrueCoach. Andy's reaction was neutral-positive and immediately practical — he redirected to portability rather than to the coaching relationship: 'having the skills to have a few kettlebells of the right weights and some routines that basically I can take my training on the road... and that's the biggest thing for me.' When the rep asked directly, the answer was flat: 'now I don't have any questions. That sounds pretty straightforward.' Scored accepted, not enthusiastic: for a prospect whose stated gap is knowing what weight to use, the video form-check and progression element was the strongest card in the deck and it drew no reaction, suggesting it was not landed against his specific problem.

anchors.raw: that's really looking at about 7,500 New Zealand dollars for me because of the exchange rate. So we're, if I still had money, because I'm from the U.S. originally, so if I still had my U.S. money, would be a lot different.
anchors.note: The single largest price amplifier in the call and the rep never acknowledged it. A USD-denominated offer lands on a New Zealand prospect at roughly 1.87x its face value. This is a structural issue for any non-US prospect, not a one-off: the number the prospect is actually deciding on is not the number the rep said.

anchors.raw: that's a substantial portion of my annual income, so I just have to think about that, right, whether or not that's something that I can swing
anchors.note: Explicit income anchor. Combined with a separation that has created two households and a recently started new job, this is a genuine affordability constraint rather than a value objection — he twice went out of his way to say he was not devaluing the offer. It is precisely the case a payment plan exists to solve, and no payment plan was mentioned.

anchors.raw: one of the things I started doing of Trevor's that I really liked was the, he's got this halo workout, it calls it 28s or something like that. And so I started doing that, and it's, that and some other things I've done, made my shoulders better, and so I'm now surfing again, and without as much pain
anchors.competitor: Primal Instinct's own free content — Trevor's online videos and the downloadable Guide
anchors.note: Self-cannibalisation anchor, and the most strategically interesting number in the call is that there isn't one: the substitute is free and it produced a real clinical result — shoulders good enough to surf again without pain. He also found the paid Guide beneath him ('My level was basically what I'd already gotten from. It's very short... designed more for somebody that was looking to start'). The free funnel is over-serving capable prospects to the point where the paid offer has to overcome its own marketing.

anchors.raw: I've got a twin brother that does this stuff professionally, and he's training me for that, you know... And so he has helped me with the program for sure.
anchors.competitor: The prospect's twin brother, a professional adventure racer, plus his 17-year-old son who is studying sports science
anchors.note: He already has two unpaid coaches in the household — a professional athlete programming his endurance block and a sports-science student advising his macros. Both were surfaced during discovery and neither was ever addressed. The rep's one attempt to contest it ran the wrong way, inviting the DIY conclusion rather than closing it: 'you could put it on your own. You could set it up, the whole program.'

anchors.raw: really it all works, it's, and none of it's easy, because what it takes is, it's consistency, you have to show up consistently, do the thing... it's not like the kettlebell's a magical tool, right... all the other stuff is, to some extent, is what flavor you want to use to get there
anchors.note: An articulated, credentialled thesis that method does not matter and only consistency does — from a man who wrote a book on training. This is the load-bearing objection of the entire call and it was raised at 00:26 in the guise of agreement, long before price. It is also, ironically, the exact argument FOR buying accountability, and the rep agreed with it instead of turning it: consistency is what the third pillar sells.

anchors.raw: can I legally expense this because that makes it a lot more affordable for me if it goes... For the business, because then it's a business expense... so the $4,000 US dollars becomes about $2,800 US dollars if I run the business
anchors.note: The one anchor working in Primal's favour, and the rep did not lean on it. If the fee is deductible as professional development the prospect's own arithmetic drops the effective cost by 30%, and he had already floated becoming a trainer, which is the justification his accountant would need. Nobody helped him build that case; it was left entirely to an email he had not yet written.

unmet_demand.want: A short, finite skills-transfer engagement — learn kettlebell programming and progression well enough to run it himself, then leave. 'When I envisioned it, it would be more doing it for a period of time until I had a good... So I don't envision me needing it for like, multiple years because I'm not trying to get in shape or anything like that.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The documented offer is 6 months at $6,000 and 12 months at $9,000, both framed as ongoing coaching. The rep improvised a three-month tier at $4,000 to meet this want, and asserted 'we have like three tiers', but a three-month product does not appear in the offer as documented. So either the record of the offer is incomplete or the rep invented a tier live on the call.

unmet_demand.want: Programming that is safe around two hip replacements with a stated dislocation risk — 'the hip socket has changed because it's artificial now. So I don't have as much surface and it can pop out more easily, and that's bad. So I have to be a little bit careful with some of the...'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The rep engaged with the hips personally but never professionally. He asked when the surgeries were, then disclosed his own need for a replacement and asked the prospect for advice, and when the training-and-mobility pillar was delivered the hips were not mentioned once; the mobility promise stayed generic ('wherever you have weak points, he will focus on that'). There is no clinical screen anywhere in the process, so nobody can say whether loaded swings, snatches and cleans are appropriate for a bilateral hip replacement, and the prospect was never told either way.

unmet_demand.want: Guidance on becoming a kettlebell trainer himself — a side business in his small town. 'I do want to build a coaching business, and so then I want some more guidance there' and 'there'd probably be an opportunity to do training, you know, to become a trainer.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The programme is one-to-one client coaching. It is not a certification, a coach-education product, or business mentoring, and nothing in the three pillars addresses teaching, cueing others, or running a training business. The rep noticed the want and echoed it back approvingly — 'maybe make a business out of it in the future' and 'side hustle, yeah? Who knows?' — without ever saying whether the programme serves it.

unmet_demand.want: Help making the fee a legitimate business expense in New Zealand — an invoice, a receipt framing, or a professional-development justification his accountant could accept.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Nothing in the offer or the process addresses non-US tax treatment or supplies documentation framed for deductibility, and the rep offered no help beyond asking when the accountant would reply. The prospect had already handed over the argument that would work — he is considering becoming a trainer, which makes this professional development — and it was left on the table.
